articles.title: Chris Paul, Russell Westbrook Go Viral With Retirement Video
articles.summary: Chris Paul and Russell Westbrook took retirement to the high seas, trading yacht alley-oops as Kevin Durant and other NBA names reacted. The post Chris Paul,...
articles.body:
Chris Paul and Russell Westbrook apparently haven't stopped throwing alley-oops just because their NBA careers are over.

Paul and Westbrook shared an Instagram video on September 1 showing the two recently retired point guards playing basketball aboard a yacht. With a hoop set up on the deck, Paul and Westbrook took turns throwing lobs to one another before finishing at the rim.

Paul's caption needed only one word: "Retirement…"

The clip quickly drew attention from around the NBA, including Houston Rockets star Kevin Durant, who had a fitting description for the pair.

"Point Gods," Durant wrote in the comments.

Kevin Durant, NBA Players React to Paul-Westbrook Yacht Clip

Durant wasn't alone in reacting to Paul and Westbrook's unusual retirement activity.

The Instagram comments filled with jokes and messages from basketball figures, with one recurring theme: Neither former point guard looked particularly interested in slowing down.

Theo Pinson joked about the yacht-mounted basket and the aggression of the finishes.

"Yo C did yall put the rim down for you I ain't never ever seen you act like that before," Pinson wrote, adding laughing emojis.

The account belonging to Josh Richardson also joined in with a retirement joke.

"Yeah good thing all 3 of jus retired this summer that's craazy," the comment read.

Cameron Payne wrote, "My boys," while prominent shooting coach and social-media personality Lethal Shooter reacted, "Damn this tough AF."

But Durant's two-word response carries considerably more history than the typical Instagram comment.

Durant and Westbrook spent eight seasons together with the Seattle SuperSonics/Oklahoma City Thunder organization, developing from young lottery picks into two of the NBA's biggest stars. They helped Oklahoma City reach the 2012 NBA Finals while both were still just 23.

Westbrook's August retirement prompted Durant to reflect publicly on his former teammate.

Durant described Westbrook as someone who led through his preparation and actions, saying that watching Westbrook's work habits influenced his own approach early in their careers.

The two now find themselves on opposite sides of basketball's retirement line. Westbrook stepped away, while Durant remains an active member of the Rockets.

Chris Paul, Russell Westbrook Begin Life After the NBA

The yacht video comes less than three weeks after Westbrook officially ended an 18-season NBA career.

Westbrook announced his retirement on August 12. The 2017 NBA MVP left the league as its all-time leader in triple-doubles while ranking fifth in career assists and 14th in points.

The 12-time All-Star announced in February that he was stepping away after 21 NBA seasons. Paul finished his career second in NBA history in both assists and steals.

That gives Paul's "Retirement…" caption a little more significance than a standard vacation post.

Paul, one of the league's most methodical floor generals, and Westbrook, one of its most explosive, spent much of their careers competing against one another before briefly becoming teammates with the Houston Rockets during the 2019-20 season.

They also ended up trading places in Houston. The Rockets acquired Westbrook from the Thunder in July 2019 in a deal that sent Paul to Oklahoma City.

Years later, their careers have ended within roughly six months of one another.

And apparently retirement basketball comes with better scenery.

The video shows Paul and Westbrook exchanging alley-oops with open water surrounding the court, producing the kind of scene that would have been difficult to imagine when the two were battling for playoff positioning and All-NBA honors.

The competition, judging by the yacht video, may not be.

articles.body: pau Gasol ha sido una de las grandes figuras del deporte español en su historia y desde su retirada, persigue el objetivo de trasladar todo lo que le ha dado el deporte y ayudar. Su carrera ha estado muy ligada a la historia de Radio MARCA y se ha pasado por 'La Tribu' para celebrar el 25 Aniversario de la Radio del Deporte. "La etapa de deportista ya terminó, pero se puede tener una influencia y un papel grande en otras posiciones y aprovechar ese éxito, ese reconocimiento y esa experiencia y ver maneras de aplicar los mismos valores que he tenido en otras cosas. Lo que me aportó el baloncesto profesional es único y especial e irrepetible y ahora lo que intento es perseguir otras metas, hacer equipo, tener ambición, tener grandes compañeros de viaje y dejar un poquito de más huella siguiendo ese lema de dejar el mundo un poquito mejor", explicó. El 3 de septiembre de 2006 en Saitama (Japón), España se proclamaba por primera vez campeona del mundo de Baloncesto tras un torneo increíble que supuso el primer gran impacto de la mejor generación que hemos tenido nunca en el deporte español: Pau, Navarro, Felipe Reyes, Rudy Fernández, Garbajosa, Calderón, Mumbrú, Sergio Rodríguez, Cabezas, Berni Rodríguez, Carlos Jiménez y Marc Gasol, formaron un equipo único. "Fue un momento muy especial, nos llegó en ese momento de madurez como grupo que fue diferencial. Fue una etapa muy bonita para el baloncesto y el deporte español. Entre todos nos contagiamos un poco: estaba Fernando Alonso, Rafa Nadal...hubo cosas que pusieron a España como un referente a nivel deportivo. Y nos hemos consolidado", recordó. La figura de Pau Gasol ha estado muy vinculada con el próximo desembarco de la NBA en el viejo continente. Como conocedor de los dos mundos baloncestísticos, el de Sant Boi fue claro al respecto. "Sigue moviéndose aunque está tardando un poquito más de lo que esperábamos. Creo que es algo que sucederá, ahora que parece que no hay tanto movimiento, en cuanto lo haya y haya anuncios importantes, todo cogerá una velocidad distinta. Creo que la llegada de la NBA a Europa abre las puertas a un modelo complementario y que le puede sumar mucho al baloncesto europeo manteniendo la tradición y la afiliación por los clubes y la cultural, pero añadiendo ese valor comercial y estratégico e importante de gestión mucho más profesionalizado del deporte que va a elevar el valor y la experiencia de los aficionados". Entre sus muchos proyectos y ocupaciones, Pau Gasol, es una de las caras visibles del Mundial femenino que arranca el viernes en Berlín y que es la gran cita del año en el baloncesto español. "Tenemos una grandísima selección, que aspira a todo como siempre con el máximo respeto con Estados Unidos. Tenemos un gran grupo que ya hizo un gran europeo. Estoy muy ilusionado y con ganas de verlas, de apoyarlas. Estaré en Berlín en las semifinales y en la final y confío en que la selección esté ahí", señaló. Gasol sigue muy cerca todo lo relacionado con nuestro baloncesto y conoce a la perfección lo que pueden estar sintiendo jóvenes como Aday Mara, Baba Miller, Sergio de Larrea o Hugo González, que han dado y darán el salto a la NBA y afrontan sus primeros pasos con la selección absoluta. "Comparar ni es fácil ni es justo, pero ellos tienen que crear su propia identidad. Tienen que crearse su propia etapa y ganarse todo lo que consigan. Tienen un muy buen talento como Sergio de Larrea, Santi Aldama, que tiene que dar liderazgo a ese grupo...Hay una buena mezcla de jugadores, pero hay mucho recorrido de crecimiento, de establecer...Cada oportunidad tienen que aprovecharla para cohesionar y crecer como equipo", apuntó. Pau forma está muy vinculado desde el final de su etapa profesional al movimiento Olímpico. Ganador de tres medallas en Pekín, Londres y Río de Janeiro, su figura siempre ha sido respetado por los atletas y por el COI, aunque dirigir el Comité Olímpico Internacional, no parece estar entre sus planes. "No es que lo sueñe y no es que sea un objetivo. Empecé esta andadura en el COI con mi experiencia como jugador y atleta con todo lo que me ha aportado el deporte. He intentado aportar y hacerlo lo mejor posible, ahora soy Presidente de la Comisión de Atletas y tengo dos años y medio en esta posición para intentar tener el mayor impacto posible. No sólo es ganar partidos, es hacerlo lo mejor posible dentro de la posición en la que te encuentres", valoró. En pocas semanas arrancará una nueva temporada en la ACB de la Pau estará muy pendiente como vicepresidente del Girona que dirige su hermano Marc Gasol. El ex pívot aprovechó para repasar los nombres propios del verano en la Liga Endesa. "El Barça con muchísimas caras nuevas y hay que ver cuánto tarda en engranar y competir. El fichaje de Pedro por el Real Madrid no es algo muy habitual, estaba Sergio con un proyecto distinto...el año pasado creo que el Madrid tiene una temporada bastante buena, pero las lesiones le pasan factura. El Madrid y el Barça tienen esa exigencia siempre de ganar títulos. Ricky está muy comprometido con la Penya y ganas de verle como al Girona de mi hermano Marc con el fichaje de McClung". Gasol se refirió también a otra de las noticias de la semana, la retirada de Leo Messi de la selección argentina. Pau conoce a la perfección al argentino. "Leo es uno de los mejores de todos los tiempos, felicitarle por una carrera extraordinaria y por su impacto y su legado. Creo que cuanto más éxito tienes en el deporte, más responsabilidad tienes en la siguiente etapa. Tiene 39 años y acaba de jugar un Mundial en el que lo hizo muy bien, que disfrute esa parte final de su carrera", finalizó.

articles.title: The Chinese mavericks looking to buck the trends in American college basketball
articles.summary: Zhang Boyuan is regarded as one of China’s top young basketball prospects. He’s weeks away from starting his first NCAA Division I season with the Louisville Cardinals. And he is not alone: more than 10 other Chinese players are set to take the same stage.
articles.body: “C’mon Bo, C’mon Bo, C’mon Bo.” Inside the training facility at the University of Louisville, strength coach Eli Foy stands on a weighted sled, adding more resistance. Zhang Boyuan, a 19-year-old player from northeast China, gives it everything he has, pushing the sled toward the end of the court as his teammates and coaches swarm around him, urging him on. That’s how their weekly strength session ends. It’s the first Friday morning of the freshman’s adventure in Kentucky – and in American college basketball. Zhang is regarded as one of China’s top young prospects. Last year, he left his home country to spend a year playing high school basketball in California, where his offensive talent stood out. Now, the 6-foot-9 forward is only weeks away from starting his first NCAA Division I season with the Cardinals. And he is not alone: more than 10 other Chinese players are set to take the same stage. The freshman is part of a small but growing group of Chinese basketball players pursuing their NBA dreams through a different route: crossing the Pacific to develop in the American college system, just as the NCAA itself is becoming increasingly global. “If I didn’t have a dream or a plan to play higher level basketball, I would not have come to the US,” Zhang told CNN Sports in a recent interview. In China, most young talents have traditionally chosen to play in the domestic league to develop their careers. Among them, Hall of Famer Yao Ming, former Dallas Mavericks player Yi Jianlian, and even Yang Hansen – selected 16th overall by the Portland Trail Blazers last summer – reached the NBA after spending several seasons playing at home. However, the introduction of Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) rules in 2021 allow college athletes to earn money while in school, making the NCAA a more attractive destination for players from around the globe, said Jonathan Givony, an NBA and NCAA draft expert. “So, seeing Chinese players come over and playing high school basketball and then college basketball, that’s another extension of this same trend,” he told CNN Sports. Where the dream began Changchun means “long spring” in Mandarin. The northeastern Chinese city is known for its industrial roots and long, harsh winters – much colder than Louisville. It was there that Zhang grew up playing basketball and watching the NBA on television with his dad, who is an enthusiastic basketball fan. At the time, the Golden State Warriors and Stephen Curry were dominating the league, and they became the youngster’s favorite team and player. Since NBA games began being broadcast on Chinese TV in 1986, the star appeal of American basketball has captivated generations across the country. For every kid who hoops in China, playing in the NBA is a dream that “can be seen, but never reached,” Jia Lei, a veteran journalist who has covered Chinese basketball for two decades, told CNN Sports. There is little doubt that Zhang had an NBA dream, too. Games had not been particularly challenging for him either in Changchun or elsewhere in China. “He has been the best in his age group,” said Jia. Zhang uses his size and quick first step to attack the basket, while also knocking down three-pointers off the catch or on the move. Representing a basketball powerhouse high school in Changchun, Zhang and his team finished third at a national tournament. At the 2024 FIBA U17 World Cup and U18 Asian Cup, he averaged over 17 points in both tournaments. But the path toward the NBA dream wasn’t clear until the Nike Hoop Summit in Portland last April. Zhang was selected to represent the World Team alongside talents from across the globe. Playing against the US team featuring some of the country’s most promising prospects, he experienced the intensity of American basketball for the first time. He scored six points in the first quarter but saw little playing time for the rest of the game, as AJ Dybantsa and Cam Boozer took control for the US. The World Team lost 124-114. “Before that game, I never thought about moving to America. My plan was to go to a good college in China,” Zhang recalled. “But just that single game changed everything.” A different path After returning to Changchun from Portland, Zhang managed to persuade his parents to send him to the United States. He spent one year playing high school basketball at the Veritas Academy in California, where he averaged 20.2 points per game against high-level competition. His performance caught the attention of college scouts, and ESPN ranked him No. 56 among the 2026 class. In the summer, he accepted an offer from Louisville, a tradition-rich team with three NCAA championships (though the Cardinals’ 2013 title was vacated by the NCAA in 2017). “I feel moved after talking to the coach for a long time,” said Zhang. “It’s a big program with a really strong history. I feel like this place could make my dream come true.” It was a Sunday morning when the freshman arrived in Kentucky with all his belongings from Los Angeles. In the evening, he met all his teammates and coaches, saying he found it “pretty exciting.” In a social post announcing the signing, Louisville coach Pat Kelsey said: “Known for playing with passion, energy and toughness, he brings great size, versatility and an advanced knack for scoring. We are beyond excited to watch Bo continue his rapid development in our system.” Louisville is hardly a familiar name to the Chinese populace compared with cities such as Los Angeles or New York, but Zhang hasn’t found it difficult to adapt. Off the court, he recently moved to a new apartment. On weekends, Zhang sometimes takes his teammates to a Korean hot pot restaurant. He also likes wandering around the city and across the Big Four Bridge. He enjoys the environment on the court, too: “Sometimes, I make mistakes during training, and my teammates will put their arms around me and tell me what I need to do differently. “As an international player and a freshman, their support has really helped me adjust to the environment.” Zhang is part of a broader internationalization of college basketball. A 2025 NCAA report said the Division I basketball tournaments “showcase international talent like never before,” with international players making up 15% of the women’s field and about 14% of the men’s. That international presence extends across Asia, with players from countries including China, Japan and South Korea making their mark on the college game. More than 10 other Chinese players, both men and women, are set to play Division I basketball for the new season. This list includes freshmen such as Purdue’s 7-foot-1 Huan Sinan, an ESPN four-star recruit ranked No. 75 nationally; Ran Kejia at Xavier University, a 2026 WNBA draft pick; and Jacob Zhu at Western Carolina. It also features more experienced players, such as junior Deng Yuting at Oklahoma State, and senior Wang Junjie, a Chinese national team regular. In China, the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) has traditionally been a primary choice for young talents – where Yao Ming won the championship before coming to the NBA and Yang Hansen won Rookie of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year in the 2023-24 season and was an All-Star for two consecutive campaigns. But for young players who are not big men like Yao or Yang, Givony argued that it is not the ideal path to flourish. “It’s just not easy for young talents to get on the floor in the CBA to play through mistakes because a lot of the shots and the possessions are going through important players,” said Givony. “So, coming to play against players in your age group in high school and in college in the US could be beneficial not just for Chinese players, but for any players that age.” For the Chinese basketball reporter Jia, the NCAA also offers higher-level competition, more physical play, and a better training environment compared with the CBA. No easy game For the upcoming season, the Cardinals have a whole new group, including experienced college players such as Jackson Shelstad, Karter Knox and De’Shayne Montgomery, all transfers from other schools. As one of the few freshmen on the team, Zhang will have to compete for playing time, but he told CNN that his priority this season is to learn. While he hopes to have some strong performances, his immediate goal is to focus on doing his job well. Givony sees potential in Zhang’s combination of size and versatility, which he noted is rare even in the US. But he also pointed out that the Chinese prospect will need to improve his shot selection, decision-making and defense to reach the NBA level. There won’t be an easy road ahead for Zhang, especially as Louisville will face some of the toughest competition in the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC), including the likes of Duke, Virginia and North Carolina. Other Chinese players before Zhang have faced obstacles of their own. Lin Wei, the CBA’s top homegrown scorer, averaged more than 20 points per game before coming to the NCAA but scored just 6.6 points per game in his first season at Oregon. Wang, who has already made impressive appearances at the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup for China, transferred this summer seeking a bigger role after averaging 20.3 minutes per game last season at San Francisco. To date, no Chinese player has made it to the NBA through the college basketball route – but the NCAA is not solely a pathway to an NBA career. “There are 5,500 players in Division I. Not even 1% of them are going to play in NBA. So, the other 99% have goals to play professional basketball outside the NBA. You can play in the EuroLeague, CBA, NBL,” said Givony. “I think the NCAA offers a platform for those leagues as well.” For Jia, who has watched generations of Chinese talents develop in a variety of ways, his hope is for these Chinese mavericks playing in America to stay. “Stay for as long as possible to push their ceiling higher, and do not return to the CBA too early if possible. Because in China, the basketball environment is just too comfortable in comparison,” Jia said. After spending the entire summer training with the Cardinals, Zhang hasn’t been back to his hometown in over a year. At the beginning of his senior year of high school in Los Angeles, his dad flew to the city and spent a couple of months to help him settle down. But for the most part, moving thousands of miles from home meant figuring out a new life on his own. “That was a big decision, because in China you can do everything easily. No need to worry about language or place,” said the 19-year-old. “But when you move to America, you gotta find a place to live. You (are going to) have problems (to solve). And you gotta think a lot.” Despite the hurdles, Zhang is determined about the path he has chosen for himself. “I just want to be a better player.”

articles.title: Se arma el Tacko en la NBA: vuelve el único gigante con más alcance (3,11 m.) que Aday Mara
articles.standfirst: Tacko Fall regresa a la NBA cuatro años después y ficha por los Philadelphia 76ers
articles.summary: Tacko Fall regresa a la NBA cuatro años después y ficha por los Philadelphia 76ers
articles.body: El gigante Tacko Fall vuelve a la NBA para buscar un hueco en el 'roster' de los Philadelphia 76ers y jugar al lado de Joel Embiid, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James... El coloso de 30 años, que oficialmente mide 2,29 m. sin zapatillas, pesa 141 kilos, tiene una envergadura de 2,50 m. y un alcance de manos de 3,11 m. (puede tocar el aro sin saltar) ha firmado un contrato 'Exhibit 10' en los Sixers junto a Jameer Nelson Jr. (su padre, Jameer Nelson Sr., ocupa el cargo de vicepresidente ejecutivo de operaciones de baloncesto de los Sixers) y Saint Thomas. Un contrato Exhibit 10 en la NBA es un vínculo laboral por una temporada, bajo el salario mínimo y sin dinero garantizado. Funciona como una cláusula de prueba de pretemporada Con sus 2,97 m. Aday Mara registró el segundo mayor alcance de manos en la historia del Combine de la NBA, sólo por detrás de Tacko Fall (3,05 m.). Tacko Fall jugó por última vez en la NBA durante la temporada 2021-22 con los Cleveland Cavaliers, y la última temporada militó en los Ningbo Rockets de la Asociación de Baloncesto de China (CBA) promediando 18,9 puntos —con un 47,5 % de efectividad en el tiro—. El mediático Fall, que tras formarse en UCF (NCAA) jugó para Boston Celtics, Main Red Claws, Cleveland Cavaliers, Xinjiang Flying Tigers, Nanjing Monkey Kings, New Zealand Breakers y Ningbo Rockets, tiene unos promedios de 2,2 puntos, 2,4 rebotes y 0,8 tapones en 6,2 minutos en los 37 partidos que disputó repartidos en tres temporadas.

articles.title: Una millonaria estrella rota escribe una carta pidiendo trabajo en la NBA: "Si leen esto..."
articles.standfirst: Victor Oladipo se ofrece en una carta a lo manager generales de la NBA para volver a jugar
articles.summary: Victor Oladipo se ofrece en una carta a lo manager generales de la NBA para volver a jugar
articles.body: Victor Oladipo trata de retomar su carrera en la NBA tras dos lesiones devastadoras, y el que jugador que fuese dos veces All Star ha escrito una carta en 'The Players' Tribune' pidiendo una oportunidad a los manager generales de las franquicias para volver a jugar. El número 2 del Draft de 2013 tiene 34 años, y no juega en la NBA desde abril de 2023 cuando sufrió la rotura del tendón rotuliano de la rodilla izquierda jugando con los Miami Heat. Desde 2019, cuando sufrió una rotura del tendón del cuádriceps de la rodilla derecha, no ha disputado más de 42 partidos en una misma temporada de la NBA. "Creo que mi cuerpo por fin está bien. Creo que todavía tengo un gran baloncesto —y, lo que es más importante, baloncesto ganador— por delante. Creo que puedo aportar valor a un vestuario de la NBA. Y lo único que pido ahora mismo es una oportunidad para demostrarlo", escribió en 'The Players' Tribune'. La pasada temporada Oladipo jugó 26 partidos en la G League con los Wisconsin Herd, promediando 13,5 puntos, 4,6 rebotes y 3,8 asistencias. Victor Oladipo, que en julio probó con los Pacers para demostrar que está físicamente bien, comparte que su inspiración para seguir jugando es su hija Nomi. "No sé cómo terminará mi trayectoria aquí. Quizás algún equipo me dé una oportunidad. Quizás ninguno lo haga. Eso depende realmente de ustedes. Pero si trabajan en la directiva de un equipo de la NBA y se tomaron el tiempo de leer esto: gracias desde el fondo de mi corazón. Y puedo prometerles una cosa, siempre, sobre mi historia en el baloncesto... desde la primera página hasta la última", compartió. En 10 temporadas en la NBA Oladipo, que ha ganado más de 126 millones de dólares, promedió 16,9 puntos, 4,5 rebotes, 3,9 asistencias y 1,6 robos de balón. "Es una historia de amor", se despidió el ex de Orlando Magic, Oklahoma City Thunder, Indiana Pacers, Houston Rockets y Miami Heat.

articles.title: FIBA le da el bronce a España en los últimos pronósticos del Mundial Femenino
articles.standfirst: Según el organismo internacional, la selección es la tercera máxima favorita por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia
articles.summary: Según el organismo internacional, la selección es la tercera máxima favorita por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia
articles.body: Las buenas vibraciones de la selección española antes del Mundial Femenino no son sólo exclusivas del equipo y su entorno. También se sienten fuera de él. Por ejemplo, quienes han elaborado en FIBA los últimos pronósticos antes del campeonato. A pocas horas del salto inicial, España está considerada como la tercera máxima favorita. El conjunto que dirige Miguel Méndez, según esa predicción, se colgaría a medalla de bronce después de superar a Bélgica en la lucha por el tercer puesto. Sería la reedición de la final del EuroBasket del año pasado. Por delante estarían sólo Estados Unidos, que podría cruzarse con el combinado español en semifinales si los dos equipos acaban como líderes de sus respectivos grupos, y Francia. En ese caso, el duelo por el oro mundial sería el mismo que por el oro olímpico en 2024. Para elaborar los pronósticos, se ha tenido en cuenta la disputa de todos los amistosos. España ganó los cinco que disputó con público y uno más a puerta cerrada frente a Alemania, que será su primer rival en el Mundial. La selección ha dejado buenas sensaciones en la preparación, aunque el equipo definitivo no se parezca mucho al del torneo, pues faltaban las cinco internacionales que militan en la WNBA. Awa Fam y María Conde se sumaron en Zaragoza y, después de un solo entrenamiento, pudieron participar en el ajustado triunfo ante China en la prórroga en el último choque de preparación. Raquel Carrera y Alicia Flórez se incorporaron a la expedición en Madrid el día antes de viajar a Berlín. Y Megan Gustafson llegó directamente a la capital alemana. Integrarlas a todas cuanto antes será clave. La ventaja de España es que es un grupo compacto, con jugadoras que llevan tiempo juntas, se conocen bien y conviven en un ambiente extraordinario que se transmite en la pista. Ya lo dijo Elisa Aguilar, presidenta de la FEB: "Hay jugadoras y selecciones muy buenas, pero el problema que tienen es que no son nosotras. No hay ningún equipo mejor que vosotras juntas".

articles.title: Which Players Would Every NBA Team Protect From an Expansion Draft?
articles.summary: The NBA appears to be inching closer to expansion.
articles.body:
The NBA appears to be inching closer to expansion.

During his annual address at Las Vegas Summer League, commissioner Adam Silver repeatedly said the league wants to decide on an expansion by the end of 2026. He didn't confirm it's a sure thing, but he did note that he's "optimistic about the future" of NBA basketball in Las Vegas.

Naturally, this quasi-confirmation got us thinking: If the league added two new franchises today , which players would every existing team protect ahead of the expansion draft? Bleacher Report tabbed NBA analysts Dan Favale and Grant Hughes to undertake this mission.

Since the NBA hasn't mapped out new expansion-draft protocols, Favale and Hughes followed the same rules that guided the Charlotte Bobcats' entry in 2004:

Each team can protect up to eight players.

Teams can only protect players who are under contract or restricted free agents. Unrestricted free agents are not eligible to be protected.

Each team must leave at least one player unprotected.

Get it? Got it? Good. Let's dole out some expansion-draft protections.

Everything for the Atlanta Hawks is pretty straightforward. They are trying to win and should first and foremost protect their best players.

Dyson Daniels' absence goes against that grain. Many will protect him over Zuby Ejiofor, Aaron Wiggins or Lu Dort.

Consider this an attempt to game the system.

Daniels is about to start a four-year, $100 million extension that pays him a flat $25 million per season. Since expansion teams only get to use two-thirds of the salary cap in their first year of existence, the bet is that neither one will want to dedicate nearly 23 percent of its spending power to a non-shooter who didn't exactly set the world on fire during his second taste of playoff basketball.

Leaving Mo Gueye unprotected is the second-toughest decision. He comes cheap, and his defense scales to so many different lineups. But he's going to miss the start of the season with a fractured left foot and is headed for 2027 free agency. Protecting the recently drafted and cost-controlled Ejiofor feels like a bigger priority.

The suddenly cost-conscious Boston Celtics are protecting their two best players (Tatum and White) and then all of their uber-cheap rotation players. This approach aligns with their (alleged) reason for trading Jaylen Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers.

Granted, it helps that they aren't exposing themselves to much damage. No expansion team is burning almost 50 percent of its spending power on a 36-year-old Paul George. He'll end up staying in Beantown.

Letting Mitchell Robinson go unprotected is riskier, but not by much. Paying $15-plus million per year for an injury-prone big man who can't play back-to-backs or log much more than 20 minutes doesn't scream "expansion-team material."

The real-life Celtics might also consider protecting Sam Hauser over Ron Harper Jr. At the same time, they may be more inclined to quarter-off Chris Cenac Jr. if they go that route.

Bleakness, thy name is the Brooklyn Nets.

Mike Brown Jr. and Egor Dëmin are the sole no-brainer selections. You could talk yourself into Brooklyn leaving everyone else up for grabs.

Of course, decisions aren't made in that kind of a vacuum. Noah Clowney, Josh Minott and Day'Ron Sharpe are all useful and cheap. Drake Powell showed enough defensively last year to hope his offense comes around. Joshua Jefferson is a cost-controlled combo forward whom the Nets just drafted at No. 28.

Some will leave Michael Porter Jr. unprotected. Newly created franchises won't want to build around a 28-year-old secondary option in the final year of a contract that pays him $40.8 million.

Better safe than sorry. MPJ is too important as an offensive cornerstone and trade asset for Brooklyn to risk losing for nothing, particularly when the alternative is protecting someone like Ben Saraf, Danny Wolf, Keon Ellis, Julius Randle or Nolan Traoré.

Apologies to Sion James, Tidjane Salaün and Christian Anderson. They received consideration for the final two spots that came down to Liam McNeeley and Moussa Diabaté.

The Diabaté situation is interesting. He will begin the year as the Charlotte Hornets' starting 5, but he's due for a raise after this season. The front office may leave him unprotected if it's worried about his next deal.

Related: That isn't much of a concern. Non-star bigs don't get paid a boatload of money these days unless the Los Angeles Lakers have cap space.

Prioritizing McNeeley over James or Salaün could be redundant. And Anderson profiles as more of a ball-handler. But McNeeley's summer-league exploits live rent-free between my ears.

Leaving Coby White up for grabs could be the move. As talented as he is, he's not a primary playmaker. Would an expansion team really use 25 percent of its allotted spending power on him? I'm skeptical. Just not skeptical enough to chance it.

The Chicago Bulls are the quintessential "Do they even want to protect eight players?" team.

If any of the selected players had more than one guaranteed year valued at over $11 million left on their deal, this list would be shorter. Norman Powell is the most expensive player whom the Bulls are protecting, and he has a team option for 2027-28. He's also mission-critical to their floor-spacing.

Josh Giddey's absence will grab immediate attention and perhaps incite rage in some corners of the internet. My advice: Chill. If an expansion team wants to devote around 23 percent of its spending power on the league's 57th- to 68th-best player, go ahead and let them.

Similar logic applies to Nic Claxton. The front office that traded for him may have different thoughts. But if I'm the Bulls, floor-spacers, recent first-round picks, cheap fliers (a la Leonard Miller) and bargain-bin contracts (hello, Tre Jones!) are my protected-player currency.

Six non-negotiables immediately board the Cleveland Cavaliers' protected-player bandwagon.

They can't even hope to imitate a contender if they leave Donovan Mitchell, Evan Mobley or Jarrett Allen unprotected. And they just acquired Peyton Watson to complete what they hope is a legit Core Five.

Letting Jaylon Tyson billow in the wind with three years left on his rookie contract would be malpractice. Meleek Thomas scored his way into our hearts during summer league…and is also insanely cheap.

James Harden usually wouldn't be at risk of getting picked. But his salary isn't that high relative to his regular-season impact and name. Protecting him also ensures he doesn't stage a full-on mutiny if he sticks around.

Depending on the Cavaliers' desire to cut their tax bill, they could stop this list at seven players and see whether Sam Merrill gets chosen. Please let the record reflect that this would be dumb.

Cooper Flagg would be the obvious pick if the Dallas Mavericks could protect only one player, but almost every decision after that has some nuance to it.

Kyrie Irving is probably tradable for positive value and is thus keeper-worthy, but that could change quickly if he doesn't look like himself coming off last year's lost season.

The choices get particularly tricky further down the list. Santi Aldama has the kind of shooting every team covets, and the Mavs just traded for him. Daniel Gafford is probably going to start, but he winds up exposed because Dereck Lively II's persistent injury issues aren't quite enough to make Dallas forget what he did as a 19-year-old. It feels like ages ago, but Lively appeared in 21 postseason games, finished sixth in Rookie of the Year voting and looked the part of a definite future starter in 2023-24.

Also notable: Former No. 1 pick Zaccharie Risacher is now a candidate to join his third team before his rookie-scale contract runs out. One of the expansion squads would surely take a shot on him, not to mention the other vets whom Dallas is leaving unprotected in favor of younger, cost-controlled, higher-upside alternatives.

The only easy call for the Denver Nuggets is making Zeke Nnaji available. With the former first-rounder's role continuing to shrink as he enters the third season of the four-year, $32 million deal that he signed in 2023, Denver might offer an expansion franchise some under-the-table sweeteners to take Nnaji off its hands.

There's probably a case for keeping DaRon Holmes II over Julian Strawther, who'll hit restricted free agency a year sooner. However, Strawther has actually featured in the Nuggets' rotation and shot 38.7 percent from deep last year. That's worth hanging onto.

Lastly, nobody should be clamoring for Aaron Gordon to be left unprotected. Though lower-body injuries limited him to just 36 games in 2025-26 as he hit his 30s, the veteran forward is still singularly important to the best version of the Nuggets.

If something more drastic happens that leads to the departure of Nikola Jokić or Jamal Murray, sure, you consider giving someone else a chance to pay Gordon nearly $104 million over the next three years. Otherwise, you hang onto him and hope he's healthy for the games that matter most.

Ebuka Okorie is the only possible snub for the Detroit Pistons. I say this as someone who is deeply enamored with Javonte Green and also grew up watching Jimmy Neutron .

Unprotecting your most recent first-round pick is always iffy. Especially with the Pistons' core only getting more expensive.

Process of elimination nevertheless gets us here.

Cade Cunningham, Jalen Duren and Ausar Thompson are behind the velvet rope for obvious reasons. Isaiah Joe and John Collins are too important to the floor-spacing and do more on defense than Duncan Robinson.

Daniss Jenkins is the only player on this roster apart from Cunningham who can dribble and shoot. Paul Reed's importance skyrocketed the moment he outplayed Duren in the playoffs Detroit dumped Isaiah Stewart. And while Ron Holland II has no clear path to breaking out without developing a jumper, he's hardly imperfect enough to punt on.

Draymond Green, Kristaps Porziņģis, Al Horford and Yaxel Lendeborg all signed deals to join or remain with the Golden State Warriors this offseason, which suggests the franchise views all of them as useful in its ongoing effort to stay relevant while Stephen Curry is still around. They're not going anywhere, even if some of the older guys might otherwise be considerations.

Jimmy Butler will miss half the season recovering from last year's torn ACL, but he's too valuable as a giant expiring salary that could be used in a trade. And to hear the Dubs tell it, they're banking on him coming back and being the same lynchpin he was before the injury.

Moses Moody is probably the most interesting of Golden State's protected players. He suffered a torn patellar tendon last season that might compromise his effectiveness indefinitely. With that said, he was in the midst of averaging 12.1 points while shooting 40.1 percent from deep when he went down. Both were career-best numbers, and Moody is only entering his age-24 season while making a team-friendly $12.5 million.

Keeping him leaves De'Anthony Melton unprotected, along with fan favorites Will Richard, Gui Santos and Gary Payton II. Painful stuff.

If Steven Adams continues to struggle to make it through a season healthy, keeping him over Marcus Smart could be the wrong call. The Houston Rockets brought the veteran guard aboard on a two-year, $12.4 million deal that shows they value his leadership, defense and willingness to shoot threes in the clutch.

The Rockets got a first-hand look at what he could do last postseason when Smart put up 14.7 points, 5.5 assists and 3.7 rebounds while drilling 13 of the 29 threes he attempted against them as a Los Angeles Laker in the playoffs. He had a significant role in sending Houston packing earlier than expected.

The bet here is that Adams' dominance as an offensive rebounder, which gives the Rockets' otherwise crummy half-court offense a chance to succeed when he's on the floor, matters more.

Even if he only manages to play half of the season, Adams gives Houston a dimension that no one else can. If Thompson and Sheppard both develop, Smart's role might not be as consequential as some imagine.

Things get interesting for the Indiana Pacers once you move beyond the starting five of Tyrese Haliburton, Andrew Nembhard, Aaron Nesmith, Pascal Siakam and Ivica Zubac.

Kelly Oubre Jr. gets the first of the remaining three spots. The depth chart needs his proven wing minutes.

Protecting Johnny Furphy could be overkill with him recovering from a torn ACL, but he showed way more two-way juice than yours truly imagined prior to his injury. Indiana is better off not leaving the two cost-controlled years on his contract to get picked off.

Jarace Walker ends up being the final inclusion. T.J. McConnell and Obi Toppin both project to have bigger roles this season, but if an expansion team is willing to sponge up the multi-year balances on their deals, the Pacers can live with it.

If Indiana isn't inclined to bet on what's left of Walker's combo-forward ceiling, count me among those who will advocate for Quenton Jackson or Jay Huff in his stead.

Among the young players whom the Los Angeles Clippers are making available, Kobe Sanders and Kris Dunn were the toughest to expose. Max Strus' recent arrival via trade meant both had to go.

The Clippers would keenly feel the loss of Dunn on defense, but Strus is a proven playoff contributor whose $16.7 million expiring salary also makes him a great trade chip.

When we initially ran through these, we projected the Clippers to make Bennedict Mathurin available. The deal he signed with the New Orleans Pelicans took care of that and made it easier to protect Jordan Miller, despite the young wing's torn rotator cuff.

Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler combine to make $120 million next year and are the franchise's clear cornerstones. Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton and Cameron Carr all joined the team this offseason via free agency and the draft, which means they're all still in the honeymoon phase and won't be going anywhere for the time being.

This exercise gets interesting at Jake LaRavia, whom we're keeping at the expense of Jarred Vanderbilt, Ziaire Williams, Matisse Thybulle, Jaden Hardy, former first-rounder Dalton Knecht and recent signee Kevon Looney. Also exposed to an expansion roster: some guy whose dad used to play for the team.

The Lakers might value Vanderbilt for his salary, which is the fifth-largest on the team and is a theoretical trade chip. But he's struggled enough to put real limitations on his value and might now cost draft assets (which the Lakers don't have) to move.

If forced to swap someone in for LaRavia, Williams makes a lot of sense. He's only on a minimum deal, but he has the big-wing profile that keeps lots of players in the league for a few extra years.

The Memphis Grizzlies tied the NBA's all-time record by using 33 different players during the 2025-26 season, making them one of the tougher teams to pin down from a keeper perspective.

Some very good vets are exposed here, led by offseason acquisition Isaiah Stewart and guard Ty Jerome, who was immensely productive in the 15 games he played for Memphis last season. Both wind up as potential departures because the Grizzlies, a clear rebuilder, have so many young options worth holding onto. In fact, they have so many that some, like tantalizing scorer GG Jackson Jr., also wind up unprotected.

Quinten Post just signed on in restricted free agency, and he sneaks in under the wire.

The clear top five on the list—Cameron Boozer, Cedric Coward, Zach Edey, Jaylen Wells and Cam Spencer—were easy enough. Beyond them, you could slot in any number of alternatives.

After the first two calls, the Miami Heat's protected-player card is a little too Brooklyn Nets-ian for my tastes.

They will cling to Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo, because duh. They'll do the same for Andrew Wiggins and Davion Mitchell, because both pass for three-and-D complements on this roster.

Miami will also put a "Hands Off" sticker on Tim Hardaway Jr., Klay Thompson and Simone Fontecchio, because shooting matters. Pelle Larsson will get one as well, because rumor has it ball-handling matters, too.

From there, all that's left for the Heat is to cross their fingers and hope one of the expansion teams' front offices mistakes Nikola Jović's name for Nikola Jokić.

Protected spots on the Milwaukee Bucks' docket run out faster than you'd think.

Brayden Burries and Nate Ament are instantly off-limits after the Bucks selected them in the 2026 draft lottery. Ryan Rollins is the closest the Bucks have to a primary building block. Kel'el Ware continues to have blue-chip-prospect sheen.

Kasparas Jakučionis was ahead of schedule as a shooter during his rookie season in Miami and has mystery-box glow as a playmaker. Milwaukee can't risk cutting bait with him when he has three years left on his rookie-scale deal.

Jaime Jaquez Jr.'s proximity to restricted free agency in 2027 complicates his importance. But he just finished second in Sixth Man of the Year voting, and the Bucks don't have a ton of combo forwards.

Choosing Tyler Herro and Ousmane Dieng over AJ Green is where it gets tough. Herro may not factor into Milwaukee's long-term plans, but he's a sizable expiring contract with some semblance of trade value.

Unprotecting Dieng and keeping Green could be the right way to go. But Milwaukee has enough guards who aren't quite wings, and Dieng popped at the end of last season.

Donte DiVincenzo is set to make only $12.5 million in the final year of his deal this coming season, which is a bargain rate for a quality starter and high-volume three-point shooter at the 2. Coming off an Achilles tear, though, he's going to miss the majority of the season and almost certainly won't be at full strength if he makes it back for the playoffs.

That's a wasted roster spot Minnesota can't afford given its aim to contend for a title after adding LaMelo Ball to its backcourt.

The Wolves just brought in Jonathan Kuminga on a new deal and intend to start him. That nudges Jaylen Clark, who also just inked a new deal, out the door.

Between the weigh-in and games-played clauses in Zion Williamson's partially guaranteed contract, the downside risk isn't nearly great enough to justify making him available in an expansion draft.

It wasn't so long ago that the New Orleans Pelicans might have felt differently, but coming off 62 games played and having just two years left on his deal, Williamson is once again a positive trade asset.

A disastrous 2025-26 campaign makes Poole's $34 million for this upcoming season one of the worst dollars-to-production deals in the league. New Orleans would be doing backflips if an expansion team removed him from the equation.

Lastly, though it's a little strange in light of him just signing, Bennedict Mathurin doesn't land among the Pels' eight protected players. Missi would probably be the one to go if New Orleans had a change of heart, but center depth is already a problem that his departure would only make worse.

No fewer than six of the New York Knicks' protected spots are sewn up without even thinking. The entire starting five has to stay put, and Landry Shamet's contract is a friggin' steal for someone who was just the seventh-ish most important player to a championship team.

Deuce McBride gets added to the list as well. He could be trade bait with free agency coming up and, thus, not long for New York. But there's a difference between moving him for something or letting him play out next season and leaving in free agency and potentially losing him for nothing right now.

Jose Alvarado, Mohamed Diawara and Tyler Kolek all vie for the final protection nod. Diawara wins out by virtue of positional scarcity and lengthier team control.

Jared McCain was a vital source of movement shooting and on-ball creation for an Oklahoma City Thunder team that always seems to need those aspects in the playoffs, but he winds up exposed for contractual reasons.

Rookie center Aday Mara was a real consideration to take McCain's place, but the Michigan product is under team control through 2029-30 before he hits restricted free agency. McCain could hit the market after 2027-28 and figures to get a significant raise.

OKC already had to jettison three rotation players to cut costs this offseason, and it doesn't project to get cheaper any time soon. Every dollar counts extra for the Thunder.

In addition to McCain, several very valuable pieces will be available for expansion teams. Jaylin Williams and Kenrich Williams will join him, along with three players—Bennett Stirtz, Thomas Sorber and Nikola Topić—whom OKC picked in the first round of the last three drafts.

Edgelords will leave Paolo Banchero or Franz Wagner unprotected. And look, if you give the Orlando Magic truth serum, they likely regret not negotiating harder with at least one of them before shelling out max contracts to both.

Hanging them out to dry in an expansion draft won't amount to a do-over, though. The flexibility gained by possibly losing one of them won't make up for the trade assets they mortgaged to acquire Desmond Bane.

To that end, Orlando's entire starting five gets a pass. While that group is less-than-ideally priced, it deserves more time than the 19 regular-season games it saw together last season.

Anthony Black's defense and ball-handling remains too important to the program. Maybe the Magic end up having to choose between him and Jalen Suggs (or someone else) before his next deal in 2027-28. Making that choice one year from now is better than having it prematurely made for you.

Orlando's shaky wing depth necessitates protecting Tristan Da Silva, who also happened to be legitimately good last year. The eighth and final spot comes down to Jamal Cain, Jase Richardson or Noah Penda. (Sorry, Goga Bitadze.)

Cain might be the best of the trio right now. But Penda is the youngest and has more positional versatility than Richardson. He gets the nod.

Tossing Joel Embiid into the unprotected ranks is more complicated than it seems.

Sure, with three years and $187.9 million remaining on his current deal, he is on perhaps the league's worst contract . The Philadelphia 76ers would love to get that money off their books.

But the front office must weigh the emotional impact of leaving him unprotected. It'd be one thing if he was guaranteed to be drafted. Given his injury history and the fact he makes up over 52 percent of an expansion squad's spending power, he probably won't get taken.

Philly should leave him unprotected anyway. General manager Mike Gansey can spin it as the Sixers playing the odds and actually roping off nine players.

Once the Embiid decision is made, the rest is cut-and-dried. As the No. 22 pick in this past June's draft, perhaps Labaron Philon Jr. has a case over Dean Wade, Anfernee Simons, Adem Bona or Dominick Barlow. It won't be a particularly strong one.

Acquiring LeBron James and Jaylen Brown in the same offseason dictates the Sixers invest everything they have in the here and now. Barlow, Bona, Simons and Wade are way more important to next year's hopes than Philon projects to be.

If I'm in charge, I think long and hard about making Devin Booker available. He isn't going to produce at a level commensurate with his average annual value of $61 million through 2028-29 (plus a $69.4 million player option in 2029-30) as he enters his 30s.

Realistically, the Phoenix Suns won't risk the PR hit of exposing Booker. It's also fair to argue they might be able to get positive value for him in a trade before his contract runs out.

Jalen Green is the biggest name left among the players whom Phoenix isn't protecting. His empty scoring doesn't justify the $36.1 million per year he'll collect through 2027-28, and that was true before he struggled to stay on the floor last season.

Reasonable minds can disagree about choosing to protect Ighodaro (the third center whom Phoenix is keeping) over Rasheer Fleming, Ryan Dunn and recent signee Luke Kennard.

Ja Morant is the easy guy to make available, both because of his substantial downside risk and the low price the Portland Trail Blazers paid to acquire him. The Blazers probably would have just wiped Jerami Grant from their books if the only added cost was doing the same with Kris Murray.

At best, Morant is a slightly negative asset. Allowing another team to make him their problem feels logical, particularly given the glut of guards already on Portland's roster—four of which it's protecting.

A year ago at this time, all the Yang Hansen hype would have made exposing him unthinkable. But he looks nowhere near ready to contribute and may not be able to his the main flaws—poor foot speed and a lack of defensive oomph—through hard work. Plus, it's too tough to make a case that the Blazers would choose to make anyone on their protected list available before him.

The Sacramento Kings haven't yet found a positive-value trade for Domantas Sabonis after at least a year of at least mildly considering proposals. That means he could credibly be included in the unprotected group. Would it really be the worst thing to scrub his remaining two years and $94 million from the books?

Realistically, exposing Sabonis would be shortsighted. He could boost his value by staying healthier this season and getting closer to the end of his contract.

If the Kings were to take a nuclear step, Sabonis would join Zach Lavine and his expiring $49 million salary.

De'Andre Hunter is another tricky potential keeper. With only one year on his deal, he could at least be used to take back a longer-term bad salary with a pick attached. So he gets to stay over Malik Monk and his remaining $42 million.

De'Aaron Fox is one of the most conspicuous omissions from any team's keeper list. He's starting the first season of the four-year, $221.7 million extension that seemed to be agreed upon the moment that the San Antonio Spurs brought him in via trade in 2025.

An All-Star last year and about to be compensated as if he's the second-best player on a Finals team, his availability might seem shocking. But if you're the Spurs, aren't you at least considering removing his money from your books and using it to sign a player at a less crowded position?

Dylan Harper is a future superstar, and Stephon Castle belongs in the starting lineup next to him. While they're both on their rookie-scale deals, the Spurs have a golden opportunity to spend big on someone other than Victor Wembanyama—and they're currently doing so on their third-best guard. Fox is not going to age well, and he's already showing up on plenty of "worst contract in the league" lists .

San Antonio could get a badly needed do-over if an expansion team snagged him.

Knowing the Toronto Raptors, they are more likely to extend Jakob Poeltl than leave him unprotected in an expansion draft. Fortunately, he's not extension eligible, so we're in the clear.

Any quibbles with Toronto's eight selections will be lower-level.

Scottie Barnes, Kawhi Leonard and Collin Murray-Boyles are expansion draft no-gos. The same should be said for Ja'Kobe Walter, who is currently the Raptors' only three-and-D wing (non-Kawhi division).

There will be those who want the three years and $97.5 million left on Immanuel Quickley's contract off the books. They're free to keep kidding themselves. Toronto still needs IQ's on- and off-ball gravity, and his salary will never account for 20 percent of the cap again.

Jump-shot limitations and all, Jamal Shead's on-ball defense has to stay north of the border. Pleas can be made on Allen Graves' behalf, but Jamison Battle's outside stroke brings more utility to a roster that continues to lack reliable marksmen.

Quite a mixed bag here for the Utah Jazz, who hang onto two high-priced stars, a soon-to-be-extended Keyonte George, two recent lottery picks and some relatively inexpensive vets.

Isaiah Collier might have made sense to keep if Utah hadn't hit the gas with the Jaren Jackson Jr. trade last season, a move that had plenty to do with George also profiling as an All-Star talent. Collier hasn't shown enough to merit being protected, but he would be worth looking at from an expansion team's perspective.

If you believe any of his stat-stuffing work during stretches of Utah's non-competitive pre-JJJ run could translate to more meaningful games, perhaps Kyle Filipowski would be worth keeping around. But the frontcourt has its top two options, and both of them are paid huge salaries. Flip's defensive issues and suspect production don't justify a keeper spot.

Trae Young's absence is calculated. The Washington Wizards seem to want him, but with a four-year, $212.8 million deal in his back pocket, they're the only ones.

Unprotecting him is Washington having its (curiously flavored) cake and eating it, too. If this strategy proves wrong, well, the Wizards front office can thank me later.

Washington could follow the same course with Anthony Davis. Even with his higher salary and injury history, though, he's viewed more favorably around the league. The Wizards should be able to get something for him if they don't want to keep him long-term.

AJ Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George and Will Riley are protected-player locks. With two years and under $6 million remaining on his contract, Justin Champagnie should be, too.

Tre Johnson is among the few players on this roster who's already an above-average outside shooter. He gets to stay even if Washington wasn't just one year removed from using a top-six pick on him.

This leaves Bub Carrington out in the cold. The issues should end there. Anyone campaigning for Deandre Ayton, Khris Middleton or Tre Mann to get one of these spots has an unhealthy obsession with 11th-place aspirations, much like the Wizards.

Dan Favale and Grant Hughes are NBA Analysts for Bleacher Report. Follow them on Bluesky, and subscribe to their podcast, Hardwood Knocks .

articles.title: Sophie Cunningham and Brittney Griner share ‘intimate moment’ amid WNBA politics
articles.summary: Sophie Cunningham divided opinion by advocating to exclude transgender women from female sports, citing a desire to protect women’s spaces. Conversely, Britt...
articles.body:
Sophie Cunningham divided opinion by advocating to exclude transgender women from female sports, citing a desire to protect women's spaces.

Conversely, Brittney Griner came out publicly early in her career and has long served as an outspoken advocate for LGBTQ+ inclusion, anti-bullying, and queer visibility.

Not that Griner has any affiliation or previous comments on transgender women, but many fans presumed that their viewpoints could put them on opposite sides of a WNBA culture war.

Sophie Cunningham and Brittney Griner moment during Indiana Fever vs Connecticut Sun

The outspoken Riley Gaines was in attendance for the WNBA clash between the Connecticut Sun and the Indiana Fever prior to the international break.

One thing that she noticed sitting courtside was the embrace between Brittney Griner and Sophie Cunningham , which she states may come as a surprise given the current politics in the WNBA.

Speaking on her YouTube channel, she said: "I think most people would have thought that Sophie and Brittney Griner wouldn't like each other. Kind of cool because I watched Brittney Griner and Sophie Cunningham like really embrace each other and have kind of like an intimate moment where clearly words were exchanged."

Her boyfriend added: "All the differences in viewpoints or whatever else, it gets put aside and it it was the it was the true essence of what sport is."

Brittney Griner and Sophie Cunningham actually shared a close bond as Phoenix Mercury teammates for six seasons (2019–2024). And Cunningham frequently expressed vocal support for Griner, publicly celebrating her return from Russian detention.

articles.title: Caitlin Clark feeling 'the best' she ever has during WNBA career
articles.summary: After dealing with a series of injuries, Caitlin Clark said this is the "best" she's ever felt during her professional career.
articles.body:
As Caitlin Clark enters the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup break on a roll, the former Hawkeye commented on her overall health status after the Indiana Fever's Friday win over the Connecticut Sun.

"I mean, I feel really good. I feel probably the best I've ever felt in my career and from like a confidence standpoint, too," Clark said.

Clark dropped 34 points in the Fever's win over the Sun and became the first WNBA player to score 30-plus and dish out 10 or more assists in consecutive games in league history.

But, it's been a process to get back to this point. Clark played just 13 games in 2025 as she dealt with a series of injuries. Then, Clark began this season with a back injury that lingered and that the Fever worked to help her manage. As a result, the three-time WNBA All-Star has still only played a total of 89 career games.

"Obviously your rookie year is a different kind of beast when you're trying to figure out the league and figure out where you fit on a team and still do the things that you can do. And then obviously lost my second year, so this is really only my second year in this league. I've only played maybe 80-plus games in this league.

"I feel like at times that can be a little lost to everybody on the outside world. I think you feel like I've been in this league for a while. I'm still kind of finding my footing and still remembering what I can do and who I am and what I can bring to this team and just having that confidence about me and allowing that to be impactful to the rest of my team. Just continuing to do that. I think it was a battle for the first 20 games for me to really find my confidence again, mostly in my body. Now, I feel like I'm just playing. I'm not thinking. I'm just like, 'Next play, next play, next play.' And that's when I play my best basketball," Clark said.

So far this season, Clark is averaging career-highs in points (22.5), field goal percentage (45.6%) and 3-point percentage (37.3%) in 36 games played.

The WNBA season is currently paused as Clark and Team USA compete in the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin, Germany.

Once the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup ends, Clark and the Fever will have just four games remaining in their regular-season schedule. The Fever (26-14) will resume play on Friday, Sept. 18 against the Toronto Tempo (11-29) at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum, with tipoff scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT on Ion.

Clark and Team USA's first contest in the FIBA World Cup is on Friday at 7:15 a.m. CT against China.

articles.title: La Liga Endesa amplía su alcance y se verá también en abierto en TVG, Aragón TV y EITB
articles.standfirst: Las tres cadenas autonómicas se unen a TV3/3Cat con una cita habitual en abierto los domingos por la mañana
articles.summary: Las tres cadenas autonómicas se unen a TV3/3Cat con una cita habitual en abierto los domingos por la mañana
articles.body: La ACB ha llegado a un acuerdo con la TVG, Aragón TV y EITB para unirse a las retransmisiones de la Liga Endesa en las temporadas 2026-27 y 2027-28. Las televisiones autonómicas de Galicia, Aragón y País Vasco volverán a retransmitir ACB 11 años después y se unen a TV3/3Cat en Cataluña para configurar una cita habitual en abierto los domingos por la mañana. La Liga Endesa se verá todas las jornadas en abierto en TVG y AGalega, en una campaña que se presenta histórica para el baloncesto gallego con la participación de Leyma Coruña, Monbus Obradoiro y Río Breogán en la Liga Endesa. TVG debutará en la primera jornada el próximo domingo 27 de septiembre a las 12:00h con el Río Breogán – Asisa Joventut, y en las tres primeras semanas visitará ya a los tres conjuntos gallegos. En la sexta jornada, el 1 de noviembre, se vivirá el primer derbi, Monbus Obradoiro – Río Breogán. Aragón TV y EITB tendrán citas habituales con la Liga Endesa las dos próximas temporadas, con 10 partidos cada una por campaña. Las retransmisiones en Aragón TV y Aragón Play comenzarán en la primera jornada con La Laguna Tenerife – Casademont Zaragoza (27 de septiembre, 13:00h) y tendrán como protagonista al equipo maño, representante de la comunidad en la acb. EITB llevará el mejor baloncesto a su universo Kirolak. En su caso, Kosner Baskonia y Surne Bilbao se repartirán el protagonismo de los 10 encuentros, con el Leyma Coruña – Surne Bilbao de la segunda jornada (domingo 4 de octubre, 12:00h) como primera cita en ETB1 y kirolakeitb.eus. El primer derbi llegará el 22 de noviembre a las 12:00h con un Surne Bilbao – Kosner Baskonia. Con estos nuevos acuerdos, el alcance audiovisual de las competiciones acb sigue creciendo en esta temporada 2026-27. Actualmente, las competiciones acb se pueden ver al completo en DAZN, con todos los partidos en directo y a la carta desde cualquier dispositivo por solo 5,99€ al mes (Plan Baloncesto). Además, también están disponibles a través de DAZN en Movistar Plus+, con dos partidos en la oferta para todos sus clientes y el resto para el paquete deportes o baloncesto, así como en Orange TV y Vodafone TV. Las retransmisiones también son accesibles mediante contratación en otros operadores OTT y de telefonía.

articles.title: “I’m just trying to understand why”: LeBron James’ $25.5M foundation faced academic criticism while creating new opportunities for Akron’s youth
articles.summary: NBA News: LeBron James’ connection with Akron goes well beyond basketball. His foundation has spent years supporting children in his hometown through education .
articles.body: LeBron James’ connection with Akron goes well beyond basketball. His foundation has spent years supporting children in his hometown through education and family programs. But the work has also faced difficult questions. The I PROMISE School came under academic scrutiny after disappointing state test results in 2023. Three years later, the foundation continues to back Akron’s children, with a new Nike partnership giving students another opportunity to learn, grow and build confidence.The latest program adds a different kind of lesson. Instead of focusing only on grades, it puts students in the pool and teaches them a skill that can stay with them for life. Poor test results put LeBron James’ I PROMISE School under serious scrutinyThe criticism became public in July 2023 after Akron Public Schools reviewed state testing data from the 2022-23 school year. The I PROMISE School, which opened in 2018 with support from the LeBron James Family Foundation, faced questions over the academic progress of its students.The numbers were difficult to ignore. No eighth-grade student at I PROMISE had passed the state math test for three straight years, according to reporting published on August 1, 2023. That result drew concern from Akron school officials, especially because I PROMISE serves students who enter school already behind academically.Akron Public Schools Board President Dr. Derrick Hall questioned the results during a July 24, 2023, board meeting. He acknowledged that the pandemic could have affected student performance, but he also pointed out that other students without the same level of resources were performing better.“I’m just trying to understand why. I think it’s fair to ask that question,” Hall said during the meeting.Hall also expressed disappointment because he had hoped I PROMISE could become a model for other schools in the district. His comments put the focus on a difficult issue for LeBron James’ foundation: providing more resources does not automatically guarantee stronger test results.The foundation did not walk away from the school after the criticism. Instead, it stressed its long-term commitment to the students and their families.“When we started this work to wrap around students through education, we entered this partnership with Akron Public School for the long haul,” the foundation said in a statement released after the test results. It also said the work required “long term commitment, hard work, and a lot of love and care.”That response is important because the foundation’s work has continued well beyond the classroom.Nike partnership gives Akron students another opportunityOn Sept. 2, 2026, the I PROMISE School highlighted its fourth consecutive summer working with Nike on a swim camp. The program gave students the chance to learn swimming while building confidence.The school said first-time swimmers worked through their fears, while returning swimmers took on leadership roles and helped their peers. The program also involved the Firestone High School swim team and U.S. Sports Camps.The latest financial records also show the scale of the foundation behind the work. Its 2024 Form 990 listed $25.52 million in total assets and $20.96 million in net assets. The foundation reported $7.53 million in revenue and $11.06 million in expenses that year, with about $9 million going toward program services.So the criticism over I PROMISE’s academic results remains an important part of the foundation’s story. But it is not the whole story. articles.title: Nets Reportedly to Hold 'Swamp Dragons' Night to Honor Nickname Change Considered in 1990s
articles.summary: The Brooklyn Nets are still in the midst of an ongoing rebuild, but they reportedly have plans for special promotions that should keep fans interested.
articles.body:
The Brooklyn Nets are still in the midst of an ongoing rebuild, but they reportedly have plans for special promotions that should keep fans interested.

Per NBA insider Zach Lowe , the Nets will be holding a Swamp Dragons night on Jan. 29 as part of a series of "eras nights" celebrating the franchise's history. The team nearly rebranded to the Swamp Dragons in the 1990s before ultimately choosing to continue on as the Nets.

In 2016, Lowe detailed an oral history of how the Nets almost became known as the Swamp Dragons. The name change was considered due to the team's status as the league's punching bag with eight losing seasons between 1990 and 2000.

"The Dragon came up right away, but we needed something to identify it locally," former team president Jon Spoelstra told Lowe. "I was sitting in my office with Jim Lampariello, our vice president, and I just said, 'Every time I look out the window here, I see this swamp. And every time I think of swamps, I think of swamp rats. What about that?' He just said, 'I don't think that's very nice. What about Swamp Dragons?' I loved it. Dragons are mythical, and fun."

However, when Spoelstra and design expert Tom O'Grady presented the idea to then-NBA commissioner David Stern, they immediately received pushback.

"David told me, 'This is the stupidest f--king idea I've ever heard,'" Spoelstra recalled.

Still, Stern allowed the Nets to move forward with their rebranding plans, first needing all seven of the team's owners to agree before getting a supermajority of the league's other 27 owners to approve the change. The Board of Governors voted 26-1 to make the change, but the one dissenting vote caused a major problem.

"David called me screaming, 'What the f--- is going on?' I asked what he was screaming about. He told me the vote came in, 26-1, in our favor. Well, that's terrific. What's the problem?" Spoelstra said. "He told me: 'No, that isn't terrific, because the one dissenting team was you -- the Nets.' We voted against our own name change. I thought he was kidding. If your own team votes no, you can't go ahead with something like this."

It turns out that David Gerstein, one of the Nets' seven owners, backed out at the last minute after rethinking his vote, though he claimed that his fellow owners also agreed to reverse course.

"I don't recall the vote, but we all thought it was inappropriate in the end," Gerstein said. "The name just wasn't right. I mean, would they be the Brooklyn Swamp Dragons today? The rest of the league would have done whatever we wanted, but we decided collectively to vote against it."

"I always thought David [Gerstein] was the Nervous Nellie of the group," Spoelstra said. "He's a terrific guy, though. After David [Stern] called me, I finally got [Gerstein] on the phone, and tried to get him to reverse his vote. He said he had just gotten nervous, and couldn't vote for it. Cold feet. I didn't even know they rotated votes."

Still, the lore of the Swamp Dragons lives on, and the Nets will celebrate the idea later this season. The "eras nights" should provide fans with some excitement in another year where Brooklyn will likely be near the bottom of the league.

articles.title: El Joventut ficha a Sebi Lapuste, el Ricky del futuro que se forjaba en Madrid e impresiona a Europa
articles.standfirst: Sebastian-Petru Lapuste (15 años) militaba en el emergente Distrito Olímpico y se quedó a dos asistencias del cuádruple doble en el Eurobasket U16
articles.summary: Sebastian-Petru Lapuste (15 años) militaba en el emergente Distrito Olímpico y se quedó a dos asistencias del cuádruple doble en el Eurobasket U16
articles.body: El Asisa Joventut se ha adelantado a grandes de Europa para fichar a Sebastian-Petru Lapuste, la sensación adolescente que el último año se ha forjado en Madrid y que ha maravillado en el último EuroBasket U16. La Penya ha fichado a Lapuste de Distrito Olímpico, el emergente club de San Blas en el que el Sebi ha impactado al baloncesto de Madrid. "¡Qué honor ha sido trabajar contigo Sebi! Orgullosos de tu evolución y logros en tu primer año en España y con ganas de ver tus siguientes pasos aunque sea lejos de Madrid. Toda la suerte del mundo en tu nueva etapa en @penya1930 una de las mejores canteras del baloncesto nacional", publicaron desde DST Factory, el programa de formación de alto rendimiento de Distrito Olímpico. El base rumano de 15 años y 1,91 m., al que comparan por su capacidad de sumar y roban con Ricky Rubio, hizo historia en el EuroBasket U16 con un triple-doble... ¡con robos de balón y a 2 asistencias del cuadruple-doble!: 34 puntos, 10 rebotes, 10 robos, 8 asistencias y 47 valoración. Lapuste (5 de septiembre de 2010) cerró el Eurobasket U16 con unos interesantes promedios de 20 puntos, 8 rebotes, 6,9 asistencias y 5 robos para 21,7 de valoración. Con apenas 15 años, cumple los 16 en pocos días, Sebi Lapuste ha sido reclutado por la agencia BeoBasket del superagente Misko Raznatovic y convocado con la selección absoluta de Rumanía. Sebi Lapuste reforzará el equipo junior y el equipo de la Liga U22 del Joventut. Sebi Lapuste, escolta de 15 años que el Joventut ha fichado de Distrito Olímpico, es la némesis generacional de Rhys Robinson, la perla de 16 años del Real Madrid que recientemente fue nacionalizado español por carta de naturaleza. El cotizado jugador romano sumó 19 puntos, 5 rebotes, 2 asistencias y 5 recuperaciones en la ida contra el Madrid y 31 puntos (fallando 9 tiros libres (10 de 19)), 7 rebotes, 8 recuperaciones, 3 asistencias y 1 tapón para 34 de valoración. "Fue una experiencia muy importante para mí jugar contra un jugador del nivel de Rhys Robinson. Es un jugador de élite, y partidos como este te obligan a mantenerte completamente concentrado en todo momento", le explicó Lapuste, que llegó en agosto de 2025 a España de la mano de DTS Factory para formarse baloncestísticamente y académicamente en Madrid.

articles.title: Russell Westbrook's Next Career Move After NBA Retirement Revealed with New Basketball Venture
articles.summary: Russell Westbrook is following up his iconic NBA playing career by getting involved in a new global basketball league.
articles.body:
Russell Westbrook is following up his iconic NBA playing career by getting involved in a new global basketball league.

Westbrook is joining Project B as co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, the organization announced Wednesday.

The nine-time NBA All-Star "will take an active role in shaping the company's basketball strategy and long-term vision," according to Project B.

Westbrook also holds an ownership stake in Project B. The men's and women's basketball league set to compete in Asia, Europe and the Americas after tipping off its inaugural season in January 2027.

The new role will involve creating collaborations with companies that Westbrook has been previously been involved with "across media, consumer products and community programming," according to Project B.

Since founding his investment company Russell Westbrook Enterprises, Westbrook has been involved in investment opportunities ranging from auto part manufacturing to artificial intelligence startups . He told Forbes' Matt Craig in 2023 his goal was to someday be a billionaire.

Spotrac reports Westbrook earned almost $350 million in salary through his 18-season NBA career, which ended Aug. 12 when he announced his retirement from playing.

Westbrook isn't the only current or former professional athlete to get involved in Project B since the league was first founded by tech executives Geoff Prentice and Grady Burnett.

The company is also led by former Atlanta Hawks general manager Landry Fields, who is serving as head of men's basketball, and former WNBA star Alana Beard, who has been hired as chief basketball officer.

Other investors have included former NFL quarterback Steve Young, women's basketball icons Candace Parker, Lauren Jackson and Cheryl Miller, and tennis stars Novak Djokovic and Sloane Stephens, per Front Office Sports' Ben Horney and Daniel Roberts and Forbes' Allison Smith .

The league has already signed current WNBA players including Azzi Fudd, Nneka Ogwumike, Alyssa Thomas, Jonquel Jones, Jewell Loyd, Kelsey Mitchell and Sophie Cunningham.

Stops on Project's B first season are set to include Valencia, Spain and Tokyo, Japan . The league has previously said each city is expected to host a 10-day tournament.
